Control laws in the Rattlesnake MIMO random environment

Reference for the six control laws and one diagnostic in control_laws/, as the code stands 2026-09-20. Written against the source, with line numbers, for someone who has to modify it.

This document describes what each law computes, in what order, with which safeguards, and what it does not control. Where a law's own docstring disagrees with its code, the code is described and the disagreement is flagged. Several sections record measured failures and their corrections, because in every case the failure is the clearest available explanation of why the code is shaped the way it is.

0. Common interface and notation

Rattlesnake offers three calling conventions. A plain function is called afresh every control cycle and holds no state. A class (control_python_function_type = 2) is constructed once, receives system_id_update() after identification, and control() every cycle. A generator is primed with next() and driven with send().

A loader detail that will cost you an afternoon Rattlesnake recognises a class as a control law only if system_id_update and control are in the class's own __dict__, not merely inherited. That is why optimal_diagonal_control_fast carries two methods whose entire body is a super() call: without them the class is invisible in the “Control Python Function” dropdown despite fully implementing both. Relatedly, control-law files are loaded standalone via importlib.spec_from_file_location with no package context, so a relative import fails outright — which is why the files that need a sibling module load it by explicit path rather than with from .control_laws import ….

Dimensions and symbols

On this article: N = 6 drives, M = 8 control channels, F = 2049 FFT lines, of which 901 are in band (100–1000 Hz). Every law is written shape-agnostically and takes these from its inputs at runtime.

Hthe FRF, (F, M, N) = (2049, 8, 6) complex. One bin's H is 8×6.
Gxxthe specification CPSD, (F, M, M), Hermitian per line.
Xthe commanded drive CPSD, (F, N, N). This is what every law returns.
Y = H X HHthe predicted response CPSD, (F, M, M).
ythe target diagonal, real(diag(Gxx)), shape (2049, 8).

The reachability problem, stated once

With 8 control channels and 6 drives, H H+ ≠ I8. The set of achievable response diagonals is the image of the PSD cone under X → diag(H X HH), and when M > N that is a proper subset of the positive orthant. A perfectly reasonable flat specification can be partly unreachable at some lines and not others. No control law gets outside that set, and a law that integrates toward a target outside it climbs until something stops it. Two channels on this rig — 13X+ and 14X+, reported as channels 7 and 8 — sit far enough outside that every law in this document gives them up; they read 10–13 dB rms in every run. §9 covers the diagnostic that quantifies this.

Three shared safeguards

Most of the laws share the same three protective mechanisms, described in full in §7 and §8 rather than repeated per law:

  • The drive-coherence cap bounds pairwise drive-to-drive coherence. It works two different ways: the optimal-diagonal family solves subject to it as an SDP constraint, while every other law post-processes it onto an already-computed solve. That distinction, not the loop type, is what predicts whether the cap costs anything.
  • The startup level cap clamps the first command only.
  • Two live-FRF guards protect the optimal-diagonal family against a diverging live FRF estimate.

1. match_trace_pseudoinverse — function, control_laws.py:520

One scalar per frequency line. The simplest law here, and the one whose limitation is easiest to state exactly.

The algorithm

The law branches on whether last_output_cpsd is None — that single test is all that distinguishes startup from steady state.

Cycle 1 (line 638–640). H+ = pinv(H, rcond) is 6×8; X = H+ Gxx (H+)H is 6×6. Because this is a congruence, X is PSD automatically whenever the specification is. The predicted response is (H H+) Gxx (H H+)H — the specification projected onto the at-most-6-dimensional column space of H. The residual is discarded, and the law neither measures nor reports it.

Cycle 2 onward (line 664, 676). c = tr(Gxx) / tr(Gyy), one complex-valued scalar per line, and X ← c · Xprev. Both traces are sums over the eight channel autospectra, so this is a power ratio. It is a pure unity-gain integrator on level: no proportional term, no rate limit, no step bound. With refresh_shape off — the default — H is never read again after cycle 1; only the level adapts while the drive shape stays frozen at whatever the startup solve produced.

Ordering (lines 688, 691, 695). Coherence cap, then the explicit level set on the refresh path, then the startup cap. The cap is applied unconditionally even though on the default steady-state path it is a no-op — a uniform positive scalar multiplies |Xij| and √(XiiXjj) equally, so coherence is unchanged — so that a mid-test law switch cannot arrive with an uncapped drive and bypass it.

Why the level is set from the final array On the refresh_shape path the level cannot simply be inherited through the coherence cap, because _cap_drive_coherence is not idempotent: its PSD re-projection moves the level by a bin-conditioning-dependent amount, and inheriting through it compounds the shift every cycle. Measured on run 01's identification with the cap at 0.95, bin 134 went +0.33 dB at cycle 5 and +28.44 dB at cycle 6, dragging a law that had been at +0.0001 dB to +2.49 dB aggregate. Setting the level from the final array also makes the constant-FRF case exact: with H unchanged the refresh path reproduces the default path bit for bit.

What it does not control

The feedback quantity is the sum over all eight channels. A line can be perfectly on-trace while individual channels are arbitrarily far off — channel 3 at +5 dB and channel 5 at −5 dB is, to this law, converged. It does not control per-channel level, response cross terms, response coherence or response phase. It has no absolute level ceiling after cycle 1, and cannot be given one: position 3 of its parameter string is deliberately skipped so that strings are not silently portable between law families.

Arguments it accepts and never reads: warning_levels, abort_levels, both noise CPSDs, both sysid CPSDs, multiple_coherence, frames, total_frames. Lines with poor input/output coherence are not de-weighted or gated in any way.

Documentation gap The law's own docstring (lines 604–609) documents three parameter positions. The parser reads five. refresh_shape at position 4 is live and undocumented there; a value passed at position 3 is silently ignored.

2. optimal_diagonal_control — class, optimal_diagonal_control.py:167

A per-bin semidefinite program, spent under a budget. The most accurate law here, and the one with the most machinery.

The formulation

Per frequency line, with X the 6×6 drive CPSD itself as the decision variable:

minimize_X   || diag(H X H^H) - y ||^2 + reg * ||X||_F^2
subject to   X >= 0                                    (the PSD cone)
             |X_ij| <= max_drive_coherence * sqrt(X_ii * X_jj)   for all i != j

Both constraints are convex — the coherence one is |affine| ≤ concave — so this is a genuine SDP with no manifold optimisation. It is built once per (M, N) shape and reused across all 2049 bins through cvxpy Parameters, rather than paying DCP canonicalisation per solve. Solver is CLARABEL.

Why H cannot be a Parameter diag(H X HH) is bilinear in H — H appears on both sides of X — which is not affine-in-parameter and so not DPP. Each channel's diagonal term is instead reformulated as a linear functional of X: diag(H X HH)[m] = real(sum(Wm · X)) with Wm = outer(hm, conj(hm)), and Wm is computed in plain numpy per bin at negligible cost.

The buzz baseline — why every bin starts somewhere sensible

A full SDP costs roughly 20–30 ms per bin, so solving the whole band up front would stall the first command by five to ten seconds. Instead every one of the 2049 bins gets a closed-form X = H+ S H+H synthesis at initialisation, where S carries the target diagonal and the survey's measured cross-term structure (or zero cross terms if no survey CPSD was supplied). Control can start on cycle 1, and the SDP budget is then spent only where the baseline is measurably bad. The baseline is deliberately left uncapped, because it draws its cross terms from an independent-drive survey and so has no dependent-drive problem to begin with.

The three-step scheduler

Each call spends at most max_bins_per_update solves — 20 by default — across three steps in order:

  1. Drifted refined bins. Already-refined bins whose H has moved more than frf_update_threshold in relative Frobenius norm since that bin's own last solve. Capped at half the budget, so that persistent or noise-driven drift cannot starve new-bin coverage. Note this step takes bins in ascending frequency order, not worst-drift first — unlike steps 2 and 3, which sort by error.
  2. Worst-error new bins. Not-yet-refined bins whose predicted dB error exceeds error_threshold_db, worst first, with whatever budget remains. A bin already under the threshold is never marked refined and is re-scanned every call, so it gets picked up later if H moves and its error rises.
  3. Stale re-triage. Already-refined bins now more than error_threshold_db worse than they were at their own last solve. Judged against that bin's own history rather than an absolute floor, because many bins — near a structural null, for instance — can never get under an absolute threshold no matter how often they are re-solved, and comparing to one would burn the whole budget forever on bins that were never going to improve.

Step 3 exists to close a specific gap: step 1's drift test is a proxy (has H moved a lot?) for the real question (is this bin's accuracy bad now?), and once every bin has been refined, step 2 can never reconsider one again. Step 3 only ever spends budget the other two did not use, so it changes nothing about a fresh start's convergence.

The dB objective, and why it is reached by IRLS here

Minimising ∑(ŷm − ym)² in linear units caps what abandoning a channel can cost at that channel's own target squared — drive its response to zero and the penalty stops growing. The solver therefore sells the hardest channels to buy the easy ones, and is correct to, given what it was asked to minimise. On this frame, with row gains spanning 3.8 to 10.3 dB, that cost channels 13X+ and 14X+ about 5 dB each.

In dB the penalty has no such ceiling. But the dB objective is not convex, so it cannot be the SDP's objective. This class reaches it by iteratively reweighted least squares instead: weight each residual by wm = ym/ŷm, which is the Gauss-Newton step for least squares on log(ŷ/y), and iterate solve → reweight → solve. Every subproblem stays a convex SDP, so the coherence-cap constraint and the whole demote-to-the-safe-path design stay intact. Weights are normalised by ym so that w = 1 exactly when a channel is on target — which keeps reg meaning what it meant before — and clipped to [0.1, 10], a 20 dB span either way, so that a channel the current iterate has abandoned by orders of magnitude cannot make the next subproblem about nothing else.

The weighting had to go in through the existing parameters Setting Wm ← wm·outer(hm, conj(hm)) and y ← w·y gives ∑ wm²(ŷm−ym)² exactly. A separate weight Parameter multiplying that expression is parameter-times-parameter, which cvxpy rejects as non-DPP — tried 2026-09-17.

What kind of loop this is

This law has been mislabelled twice, in opposite directions. Reports before 2026-09-17 called it a feedback law. The correction made then called it open loop, and that over-shot: it understates the law just as badly, because it reads as though the plant model were frozen, when re-solving against a moving FRF is the whole of the 2026-09-19 work. Two separate loops are at issue and the label has to name both.

Closed on the identified plant model. Both control() and system_id_update() hand the live transfer function to _refine_batch every cycle. Step 1 re-solves bins whose H has moved more than frf_update_threshold since that bin's own last solve. Step 3 re-solves bins whose predicted error has degraded, recomputed against the current H, worst-first. Step 3 is the one that matters for a plant whose FRF changes with level: the drift can sit well under the gate and still be caught, because the error is always re-evaluated with the new H rather than compared to the gate. This is what runs 29, 31 and 32 demonstrated — 17.03, 18.44 and 16.22 V² with the FRF update on, against 153, 485 and 245 V² with it off.

Open on the response error — until 2026-09-21, unconditionally; now only while response_trim_gain is 0, which is the default. The solve minimises the predicted response diag(H X HH) against the target. With the trim off, last_response_cpsd is accepted and never read, and last_output_cpsd is read in exactly one place — as a boolean “is this the first command” flag for the startup cap. Any error the FRF does not explain is therefore invisible: bias in the H1 estimate, extraneous input, drive clipping, a nonlinearity that never appears in a linear FRF. There is no integral action, so such an offset simply stands.

The accurate one-line description is an indirect adaptive (self-tuning) regulator: fast model update, optional slow error trim. The self-consistency diagnostic printed each cycle is the instrument for telling the two halves apart — if the law's own predicted error stays near 0 dB while Rattlesnake's measured Response Error panel stays high, the gap is model mismatch, not a bug in the scheduling or the SDP, which would be self-consistent by construction.

The response-error trim — closing the second loop

_update_response_trim carries a per-bin, per-channel multiplicative correction t on the solver's target, integrating the measured error. Off by default (response_trim_gain = 0), in keeping with every other behaviour change in this file: with the gain at zero the trim array is never allocated, _eff_target returns the specification slice itself, and the command is bit-identical to the code before the trim went in — verified on real run-29 data, max |new − committed| = 0.000e+00.

Which error signal, and why it is not the obvious one. The tempting choice is measured-versus-predicted, 10log10(z/p), since that is literally the model mismatch. It does not work as an integrator input. For a constant multiplicative plant bias b it reads 10log10(b) for ever, whatever the trim does, because shrinking the target shrinks prediction and measurement together. It is a mismatch readout, not an error: driven by it, the integrator runs to its clamp and stops, and the clamp happening to sit at the right value would be a coincidence rather than a design. The trim therefore integrates measured-versus-specification, 10log10(z/S) — the quantity the test is judged on and the one Rattlesnake's own Response Error panel displays. It converges geometrically to t = 1/b, at which point the measurement sits on specification.

The solver-agreement gate, which is what stops the wind-up. Integrating measured-versus-specification on its own would wind up at every bin the plant cannot reach. This frame is rank 5 with six drives; at a structural null the law lands short of specification however much is asked of it, the error never clears, and a plain integrator would climb to its clamp demanding drive that buys nothing. So the trim is applied only where the solver reached what it aimed at — |10log10(p/target)| ≤ response_trim_gate_db, both sides cached from the cycle that issued the command, after the startup cap. A shortfall the solver itself predicted is an achievability limit and is none of this loop's business. Only the part the solver believed it had and did not get is model error.

The gate has its own threshold, and run 35 is why. It first reused error_threshold_db (1.0 dB), on the reasoning that the scheduler's “worth refining” bar and “the solver reached what it aimed at” were the same question. They are not. Reconstructing this law's own per-bin prediction from run 35's saved FRF and drive and comparing it with the measured response, the model mismatch on that plant is 0.060 dB rms across all 7208 in-band channel-bins. Yet at a 1.0 dB gate, 43.6 % of gated channel-bins sat outside the deadband on an error of 0.541 dB rms — thirteen times the mismatch. The trim would have spent the whole run integrating the solver's own sub-threshold shortfall, second-guessing the optimiser that is already trading those channels against each other, and logging it as model correction. At 0.5 dB, the default, only 1.6 % clear the deadband. A real bias still opens the gate exactly as wide, because the shortfall is predicted-versus-target and computed entirely from H and X: a plant that does not match H cannot narrow it.

How fast it acts. The per-channel part of the correction rides the ordinary scheduler: a changed target shows up in _err_db against the current H and step 3 picks those bins up worst-first, at the refinement budget's pace, which across 901 in-band bins is slow. The common part of each bin's change is therefore applied straight to the stored drive CPSD instead. Scaling X by a positive scalar scales diag(H X HH) by exactly that scalar, so the overall level correction — the dominant term, and the one an operator notices — is exact and immediate, and only the channel-to-channel shape waits for a re-solve. A real positive scalar leaves drive coherence and rank untouched, so this cannot walk around max_drive_coherence or drive_rcond.

Guards. A per-cycle clamp (response_trim_step_db, 0.5 dB) and a total authority clamp (response_trim_limit_db, ±3 dB) bound it; a deadband (response_trim_deadband_db, 0.5 dB) keeps it off the frame-to-frame scatter of a short-average CPSD; scoring is in-band only, since out of band there is no drive energy and the measured diagonal is noise. Because components/data_collector.py divides every acquired frame by the current test level, everything the law sees is referred to full level and the ratio is level-consistent in steady state — but not across a level change, where a frame spanning the ramp is normalised by the wrong number. A set_test_level_db hook, which Rattlesnake already calls on every change, stands the trim down for three cycles and discards the stale pairing. The accumulated trim is kept.

Measured offline (verify_response_trim.py, four tests). Against a plant 2.0 dB hotter than the model it was handed: on the channel-bins the solver reached, rms error 2.09 dB → 0.27 dB, with the trim settling at −1.76 dB and stopped by the deadband, in twelve updates. At provably unreachable channel-bins — two response channels given the same row of H and targets 10 dB apart, so the solver's own shortfall is a median 5.00 dB — the trim held at exactly 0.0000 dB. The first test is the one that had to hold: with the gain at 0 the command is bit-identical to the pre-trim commit on real run-29 data, max |new − pre-trim| = 0.000e+00.

On the rig: half-tested. Run 35 confirmed the default path — zero occurrences of either trim log line across a full run, so the trim is provably asleep inside the framework and not merely in a harness — and it is the run that set the gate threshold above. The trim has not been run with the gain on. Run 35 also shows why that run will be undramatic: with a model mismatch of 0.060 dB rms there is almost nothing on this plant for an error trim to correct, so the pending run 36 is a does-no-harm test. A plant whose FRF genuinely moves with level is what would actually exercise this loop.

Solver failure

If the first SDP pass returns no solution, the bin falls back to a diagonal-only pseudoinverse synthesis, which silently abandons both the survey cross terms and the coherence cap, and the bin is still marked refined. A failure on a later IRLS pass keeps the last good solution and is not counted. cum_solver_failures in the log counts only the first kind; it read 0 on every healthy run in this campaign and 176 on run 30.

3. optimal_diagonal_control_fast — subclass, optimal_diagonal_control_fast.py:138

The same objective, solved by factorisation instead of by cone programming, when it is safe to do so.

The factored solve

Write X = L LH with L ∈ ℂN×r. Two things follow: X is PSD and rank(X) ≤ r by construction, so the PSD cone constraint disappears entirely rather than being enforced by an interior-point method; and the problem becomes smooth and unconstrained, which is what makes it fast. The objective is the base class's minus the coherence cap, which the factorisation cannot express:

min_L  || diag(H L L^H H^H) - y ||^2 + reg * ||L L^H||_F^2

Optimised by L-BFGS-B with an analytic Wirtinger gradient ∇L = 2(∂f/∂X)L, verified against finite differences. The predicted diagonal is formed as ∑j|(HL)mj|², never by materialising H X HH — an 8·6·r product instead of an 8·6·6 chain, which is what makes each function evaluation cheap. Warm start is the top-r eigenpairs of the buzz solution for that bin.

Tolerances are deliberately loose: maxiter 50, ftol 1e-9, gtol 1e-7. At tight tolerances about 70 % of real bins hit a 200-iteration cap without visibly improving dB accuracy. Loosening cut time 5.7× — 18.7 to 3.3 ms per bin — for +0.4 dB mean and +2.7 dB worst-case against the SDP's own accuracy. Net speedup on real data is about 3.6×, much more modest than the 18–20× that synthetic-random-FRF benchmarks suggested, but honest.

The demotion gate

The unconstrained factored solve can drive pairwise drive coherence toward 1, which would make a live H1 estimator's reference CPSD matrix singular. That is fine if nothing is re-estimating H, and unsafe the moment something is. Rather than trying to detect the GUI checkbox — control()'s signature does not expose it — the law watches the safety-relevant property directly: has H moved since the last call, by more than frf_update_threshold in relative Frobenius norm? If it has, every bin for the rest of that call uses the base class's coherence-capped SDP. The decision is latched once per call.

This gate has been wrong twice, in two different ways First, it was bitwise equality, and the docstring claimed that with the FRF update off H is “set once and never re-passed”. That is not what Rattlesnake does: it passes a transfer function to control() every cycle in both regimes, and system_id_update() is never called during control at all. With the update off the array happened to be the same frozen array each time, so the fast path ran — the right outcome by the wrong mechanism. With the update on, every bin fell through to the SDP and the law was byte-for-byte the base class. Second, once it became a relative-change test, the norm was taken over the whole 2049-bin array. 1148 of those bins are out of band, where there is no drive energy, the live estimate is noise, and the relative change per cycle is unbounded. Measured over the whole array the metric read a median of 4.37 — a 437 % change every cycle — against the base class's in-band-only drift metric reading 0.17 on the same data. A factor of 25 between two measurements of the same quantity, and the reason runs 21 and 28 demoted on 99 % of cycles.

Masked to in-band bins, the measured per-cycle movement on this rig is median 0.196, 90th percentile 0.232, with a thin tail to 3.5. The default threshold was raised from 0.05 to 0.5 on 2026-09-19, which sits at about the 95th percentile: roughly 5 % demotion. At 0.05 the gate was below essentially the entire distribution, so it was always open — and because the same parameter drives the base class's drift step, every previously refined bin also counted as drifted, so half the refinement budget went to re-solving old bins forever. Changing the default altered no archived run: every profile spreadsheet sets the field explicitly.

drive_rcond — the realizability constraint

The factored path has no coherence cap and, before 2026-09-18, nothing else constraining it either. Left unconstrained it buys accuracy with drive pushed down near-null directions of H. The resulting solution is not wrong — it is unrealizable: its accuracy lives in cancellation between drives that survives only if the drive is reproduced to a precision no rig delivers.

_restricted_basis takes the thin SVD of the bin's H, keeps the k right-singular directions with σ ≥ rc·σ₁, solves in that basis and maps back by congruence, so the drive is forbidden from having any component along the plant's weakest directions.

_effective_drive_rcond derives rc from the plant itself. A positive drive_rcond is read as a multiple of the smallest structural singular direction; a negative value is an absolute ratio. Finding “structural” is the interesting part: this frame is rank 5, and its measured in-band median ratios run 1.000, 0.319, 0.084, 0.032, 0.015, 0.0017. That last value is the identification noise floor, not a direction the plant has, so scaling off σmin would track how good the system ID was rather than how the structure is conditioned. The reference is instead found by the largest gap in the spectrum — 8.9× between σ₅ and σ₆ here, against 2.1–3.8× everywhere else — and taking the smallest direction above it. Default multiple 2.0 gives 0.030 on this frame, which is the value the rig sweep found independently.

The same out-of-band mistake, a third time The singular-value spread was also first measured over all lines, which moved the reference from 0.0152 to 0.1435 — a factor of 9, the difference between the tuned 3.0e-2 and a useless 0.29. Out-of-band lines are not controlled and are conditioned quite differently. The rule now stated in the code is: any statistic taken over the FRF array on this rig must be masked to in-band bins. It has been got wrong three times — the singular-value spread, the gate metric, and the divergence guard — each written after diagnosing the previous one.

4. match_diagonal_congruence — class, diagonal_congruence_control.py:233

match_trace's one scalar, generalised to N independent knobs, with the validity guarantee kept. The only genuine feedback law in this document besides match_trace.

The idea

match_trace multiplies the whole drive CPSD by one positive scalar. That is why it is robust — a uniform positive scalar can never turn a valid drive CPSD into an invalid one — and why it is limited: if channel 3 is 5 dB high and channel 5 is 5 dB low, the trace is correct and the law does nothing at all. Replace the scalar with a diagonal congruence:

X <- D X D,    D = diag(exp(u_1) ... exp(u_N)),   u real

Congruence preserves positive semidefiniteness structurally: for any vector v, vH(DXD)v = (Dv)HX(Dv) ≥ 0 whenever X ≥ 0, because D is real diagonal. There is no condition on D at all — the gains can be arbitrarily wrong, the FRF can be badly estimated, and the commanded CPSD is still a physically realizable drive. What is gained over match_trace is N independent knobs instead of one, which is what per-channel correction requires. match_trace is the special case D = √c·I, and the degeneracy is exact: every row of the sensitivity matrix sums to 2, so when the error is the same on every channel the solution is ui = ε/2 for all i — the law reproduces match_trace's update exactly and degrades gracefully to the law it generalises.

The per-line step

Everything is a batched solve over the frequency axis — 2049 independent 6×6 solves per cycle, no Python loop over lines.

  1. Measured log error εm = log(targetm/achievedm), natural log, from the diagonal of the measured response CPSD. A channel measuring non-finite or non-positive this cycle is dropped from the solve rather than driven to zero.
  2. Model sensitivity Smi = ∂log(ym)/∂ui = 2·Re(Hmi(XHH)im)/ym, an 8×6 real matrix per line, where y is the model-predicted response. Note the hybrid: the error is measured, the sensitivity is modelled.
  3. Ridge least squares (STS + λI)u = STε with λ = ridge·tr(STS)/N — scale-relative, so a line with tiny FRF gain gets the same relative regularisation as a strong one. Eight equations, six unknowns; the solution is the best 6-DOF fit to the 8-channel error.
  4. Gain and resonance schedule. u ← Kiu times a per-line factor 1/(1 + s(peakiness−1)), because a resonance carries dynamical phase lag and has a much lower safe gain than a flat line.
  5. Step limit, enforced on the response. Clamping u itself does not bound the response move: each row of S sums to 2, but individual entries can be large and of opposite sign, so a bounded gain vector can still swing one channel a long way. The limit is therefore applied to the exact predicted per-channel log response change, with u scaled back and re-checked up to six times because the map from u to response is exponential, not linear.
  6. Command, ceiling, floor, coherence cap.

H enters only as a direction

In the feedback path H is never inverted — it appears only in forming the sensitivity, so a mediocre FRF still yields a usable direction and the feedback cleans up the rest. That is precisely what a pinv-based law cannot do, and it is where the earlier drive-imbalance events came from. The only pseudoinverse in this law is in the startup solve.

The ceiling is the anti-windup, and it is deliberately asymmetric

Two estimates of the response level are formed. The measured-anchored one is achieved × exp(move): the absolute level comes from the measurement and is therefore model-free, with only the small, already-bounded step extrapolated through H, so even a badly wrong FRF can distort it by at most max_step_db. The model-predicted one is used only where this cycle's measurement cannot be trusted, and its net is set 20 dB looser.

Why the measurement replaces rather than combines Where the measurement is trustworthy it replaces the model estimate. Taking the stricter of the two looks conservative but is not: a model that overestimates the response then holds the drive down forever and the test never reaches specification — a functional failure dressed up as caution. The 20 dB model margin exists because “the FRF is wrong by 30 dB” and “a control accelerometer has failed low” produce identical evidence, and no amount of cleverness distinguishes them from those two signals alone. A choice is forced, and this is it.

The ceiling is exempt from the step limit: coming down from an overshoot is a safety action and happens in one cycle, not over the many cycles a step limit would impose.

Aiming at what is reachable

The law optionally accepts a projected target — the closest reachable response, computed offline by achievable_response.achievable_diagonal — and drives to that instead of the raw specification, because integrating toward an unreachable target is how the earlier resolve laws reached their anti-windup ceilings. The file is read on the first control cycle, not at construction, because Rattlesnake builds the law before system identification runs so the projection cannot exist yet. Every failure mode — no path, missing key, unreadable, wrong shape — falls back to the raw specification with a message and never raises. A stale projection is not detected. It is tied to the FRF it was computed from and must be regenerated after a new system ID; nothing checks this.

What it cannot control

A diagonal congruence leaves drive coherence and drive phase exactly invariant: |DiXijDj| / √(Di²Xii·Dj²Xjj) reduces to the original coherence. The law can only redistribute power among the six drives; the entire correlation structure is inherited from the startup solve. It also does not touch response cross-spectra — the error is built only from the diagonal — and it reads no coherence or frame-count information at all.

An inconsistency worth knowing about The startup path's own comment states the principle that the safety ceiling must go last, because the floor and the coherence cap can both raise level back through it. In the feedback path the order is the opposite: ceiling, then floor, then coherence cap. No comment explains the asymmetry. It may be benign — in the feedback path the incoming drive is already capped, so the cap is close to a no-op there — but it is not documented either way.

5. pseudoinverse_control — function, control_laws.py:248

The bare least-squares solve, recomputed identically every cycle.

X = H+ Gxx (H+)H, a congruence so X is PSD automatically, with the predicted response being the specification projected onto the column space of H. The solve reads only the specification and the FRF. It never reads the measured response, has no state, and cannot converge — it lands wherever the current FRF estimate puts it and re-lands there every cycle. With the FRF update on it tracks the plant model, never its own error.

Two documentation defects in this law, both live The docstring says running_ceiling_db defaults to +3.0. The code default is 1e9 — off. So by default this law has no level bound at all from cycle 2 onward. The parser's own docstring has it right and explains the reason: a default-on ceiling would have clamped runs 09 and 11 and made the twelve-run comparison set unreproducible. Separately, the Notes claim last_response_cpsd is “accepted and never referenced”. Since the running ceiling was added it is referenced — but only to scale down, so the substance of the claim (not closed loop) survives while the literal wording does not.

The running ceiling, when switched on, carries the same measurement-anchored estimate the congruence law uses, for the same reason: a model-only ceiling uses the same H the law just used to build the drive, so it is blind in exactly the direction that hurts. On run 01's identification, with a +3 dB ceiling engaged and an FRF understating the plant by 12 dB, this law and buzz both sailed to +14.3 dB of true response and reported no problem.

6. buzz_control — function, control_laws.py:1183

pseudoinverse_control with the target's cross terms replaced by the ones the rig actually produces. One line of difference, and it is worth 1.1 dB and a third of the drive.

Per line, build a new target whose diagonal is the specification's and whose off-diagonal structure is copied wholesale from the measured system-identification response:

S~_ml = exp(i*phi^sysid_ml) * sqrt( coh^sysid_ml * S^spec_mm * S^spec_ll )

then solve X = H+ S̃ (H+)H exactly as pseudoinverse_control does. A written specification usually gives only the eight autospectra, with cross terms zero or arbitrary — and those cross terms decide how much of the target lies in the six-dimensional space H can reach. Borrowing the structure the plant naturally generates means asking for something the plant can generate.

Two failure modes to know about The survey is frozen at system identification and does not refresh during control; only the FRF adapts. And under the CVA estimator, sysid_response_cpsd is diagonal-only with zero off-diagonal terms — so the borrowed coherence is identically zero and buzz silently degenerates to targeting the bare diagonal with no cross terms, i.e. to something close to plain pseudoinverse. This is documented in the spectral-processing code, which names match_coherence_phase explicitly.

Also worth knowing: only the function form carries the safety machinery. The generator and class variants of buzz ignore extra_parameters entirely — no rcond, no coherence cap, no startup cap, no running ceiling. If a run is configured with control_python_function_type 1 or 2, none of the guards in §7 exist.

7. The startup level cap and the drive-coherence cap

On the first control cycle no measured response exists, so a law falls back to a raw solve on whatever FRF the spectral processing has produced — which on the first frame is a single noisy unaveraged estimate under both exponential and linear averaging, because there is no minimum-frames gate before an FRF is published and handed to the control law. On real hardware this was observed to overshoot by several decades.

What the cap does

Per frequency line, with the predicted response Y = H X HH:

s = min(1, 10^(cap_db/10) * tr(spec) / tr(Y)),   X <- s*X

Both sides are response-domain powers, so the ratio is dimensionless. The min(1, ·) makes it strictly a reduction — a positive cap value does not raise a command that is already low. Default −9.0 dB; 0 dB means full spec-match. It is disabled by a large value, and the implementation deliberately uses a numpy float rather than a Python one so that an absurd value like 1e6 gives +inf rather than raising OverflowError.

It binds on the first command only, in every law that has one, gated on last_output_cpsd is None. For the optimal-diagonal family the clamp is applied to the returned command while the stored solution is left unscaled, so the SDP refinement is not dragged down with it.

The two bugs, both silent

Units. The clamp originally compared the specification trace, in response units squared, against the drive trace, in volts squared. That ratio is not dimensionless; its value tracked plant gain and response-channel units. On run 01's identification the raw solve sat at −2.04 dB re specification, the clamp as written took it to a median −18.88 dB, and the corrected clamp lands on −9.00 dB exactly — roughly 10 dB too aggressive, and unit-dependent on top of that.

Order. Both callers ran the coherence cap after the level clamp, which lifted the level straight back through it. Measured with the clamp correct and the cap at 0.95, the first command came in at +6.72 dB re specification for match_trace and −0.12 dB for buzz, with worst single lines at +22.41 and +16.53 dB, against a −9.00 dB ceiling. Uncapped, both hit −9.00 exactly. The mechanism: the coherence cap shrinks off-diagonal drive terms while preserving the diagonal, which destroys the inter-drive cancellation the pseudoinverse solve relies on, so the same drive produces far more response.

The drive-coherence cap itself

For each line and each of the 15 drive pairs, if |Xab|/√(XaaXbb) exceeds the cap, the cross term's magnitude is shrunk to the cap while its phase is preserved exactly and both diagonals are left untouched; if anything changed, the matrix is re-projected onto the PSD cone by clipping negative eigenvalues. Note the comparison is against the magnitude coherence, not the squared one: 0.95 means γ = 0.95, i.e. γ² = 0.9025. A value of 1.0 or more is an explicit no-op that returns the input unchanged.

The re-projection is why the cap is not idempotent and why it can move the level — the fact that drives the ordering rules above.

The cap means two different things The optimal-diagonal family solves subject to the cap, as a constraint inside the SDP, so the solution is optimal given the constraint. Every other law post-processes it onto a finished solve, which is a projection, not an optimisation — it takes a solution that depended on particular cross terms and edits those cross terms. That distinction, not the loop type, is what predicts whether the cap costs anything.

8. The two live-FRF guards

Added 2026-09-19 to optimal_diagonal_control and therefore inherited by optimal_diagonal_control_fast and octave_band_switching_control. Not inherited by match_diagonal_congruence (a standalone class) or match_trace_pseudoinverse (a plain function).

Guard 1 — refuse an FRF that is no longer a plant model

When the FRF update is on, Rattlesnake republishes an incrementally averaged estimate every cycle — and that estimate is formed from the drive the control law itself commands. A bad solve therefore feeds a bad estimate which feeds a worse solve. Run 30 closed that loop: the live FRF reached a median 39,834× and a maximum 500,217× its system-identification value, the law solved against it, and commanded 1.8×105 V.

The guard tests, per bin and in band only, ‖Hlive − Hsysid‖ / ‖Hsysid‖ > 10. A failing bin reverts to its system-ID value for that call. It is not latched and recovers by itself as soon as the live estimate comes back inside the limit. Per bin rather than globally, so one wild line cannot condemn the whole array and the law keeps controlling on the bins that are still sane.

The limit of 10 has an order of magnitude of headroom over anything measured on a working run — run 28 logged a median of 0.1752 and a maximum of 0.8920 over its whole length — and still catches run 30 at its 55th call.

Guard 2 — break out of the zero-drive absorbing state

Run 30's end state could not recover on its own: corrupted H produced a near-zero commanded drive (0.0015 V), which meant no excitation, so the live FRF stopped moving, so nothing tripped the drift threshold, so no bins were scheduled, so the law kept commanding the same dead solution — seventy consecutive calls with every scheduler field zero and a bit-identical self-prediction. Restarting requires excitation the law is no longer commanding.

Detection is deliberately narrow: the predicted response trace must be 20 dB below the specification trace and no bin may have been scheduled, for ten consecutive calls. A working run sits within a few dB of target, so this cannot fire on one. Recovery discards the corrupted state entirely and rebuilds the buzz baseline from the system identification — the one plant model known to be good.

What the guards are not Neither guard explains what made the estimate diverge; they stop the law amplifying it and say so in the log. The demotion gate, notably, worked throughout run 30 — demoting 69 % of calls — and did not help, because falling back to the safe solver cannot rescue a solve when the plant model is wrong: both solvers get the same bad H. The gate protects against solver fragility, not estimator divergence.

Field record to date. Verified offline that on ordinary 3 % averaging jitter neither guard fires and the control output is bit-identical to the pre-guard code. On the rig they have only fired on the startup transient: run 32 on calls 7, 8 and 9 covering 4, 20 and 3 in-band bins, and run 34 on call 7 covering 15. Two different laws, the same call numbers, the same handful of bins — that excursion is a property of the rig's startup, not of either law. Run 30 remains the only divergence and its trigger is unexplained.

9. achievable_response — a diagnostic, not a control law

Answers the question every other section depends on: how much of the response error is the control law's fault, and how much is simply not reachable with this structure and these shakers?

Per line it minimises, over X ≥ 0, the dB error between diag(H X HH) and the target, returning both a best RMS and a best minimax figure — the latter being the honest ±X dB floor. Errors are in dB rather than as a linear residual deliberately: a linear residual, which is what the SDP minimises, implicitly weights the loudest channels hardest, and on a spec with any dynamic range across channels that is not the quantity the test is judged by.

It uses the same Burer-Monteiro factorisation as the fast law, with the pseudoinverse solution as its first starting point — the solution the existing laws use — so the floor search starts from the incumbent answer and can only improve on it. It also returns drive_trace, which turns “mathematically reachable” into “reachable with these shakers”.

restrict_rcond is the parameter that makes the floor comparable to a real law: it confines the drive to the retained right-singular subspace, so the floor can be computed under the same truncation the law actually uses. This separates how much accuracy is lost by discarding near-singular directions, a deliberate safety choice, from how much the law is simply leaving on the table.

The floor is not a constant — measured 2026-09-20 Computed at restrict_rcond = 1e-3 over all 31 runs, the floor is not a property of the rig: it tracks the identification. On most runs the sixth singular value sits near 1e-4, well below the cutoff, and the floor lands between 3.13 and 3.92 dB. On runs 15, 23 and 26 the identification lifted σ₆/σ₁ above 1e-3, the solver got a sixth drive direction, and the floor collapsed to 1.83–2.14 dB. “Error against the floor” is therefore not comparable across runs whose identifications differ in quality. The sixth singular value is identification noise, not structure — which is exactly why drive_rcond locates the structural floor by gap detection instead.

One detail worth knowing before consuming the output: achieved, drive_trace and drive_cpsd all come from the RMS-optimal point, while best_minimax_db comes from a different point whose drive is not returned. A consumer projecting a specification onto achieved — as the congruence law's projected target does — is projecting onto the RMS optimum.

10. Parameter reference

Every law parses its parameters positionally from one comma-separated string, and every parser swallows a malformed field and falls back to the default without warning. A typo degrades silently. Note also that position 3 means different things to different law families, which is why match_trace deliberately skips it.

11. Corrections recorded in the code

These are kept because each one is a caution about a metric or an assumption, and because in several cases the wrong version had already been reported as a result.

  • The demotion gate was bitwise equality, and the docstring's account of when Rattlesnake re-passes the FRF was wrong. Consequence: with the FRF update on, the fast law was byte-for-byte the base class, so any comparison of “fast” against “optimal diagonal” in that configuration was a law against itself.
  • Three statistics were taken over the whole FRF array rather than in band: the singular-value spread (reference moved 0.0152 → 0.1435, a factor of 9), the gate's movement metric (median 4.37 against a true 0.17, a factor of 25), and the divergence guard (fired on ~1050 of 2049 bins every call while controlling perfectly). Each was written after diagnosing the previous one.
  • The startup cap compared incompatible units and ran in the wrong order relative to the coherence cap. See §7.
  • drive_rcond was briefly gated to the dB error domain only, leaving the factored path unconstrained in its default linear mode. Run 22 is what that cost: +14.29 dB measured against −0.39 predicted.
  • The rcond cache could be poisoned by a single bin. A harness calling _solve_one_bin directly computed the singular-value reference from the one bin it was handed and cached it forever — found when an FRF sensitivity test reported 10.34 dB for a configuration the control loop scores at 5.95.
  • A constructor ordering bug in the fast subclass was latent: state was set after super().__init__(), which can reach the overridden _solve_one_bin. It never fired in the app because Rattlesnake builds laws with no FRF, and fired immediately in a harness that supplies one.
  • “Run 13 had a weak system identification” was retracted. The claim compared run 13's channel-7 minimum against other runs' non-channel-7 minima. Channel 7 sits between 0.28 and 0.54 in all thirteen identifications taken on this system — a property of the rig at the band edge. Scored like against like, run 13's identification was the best of the set. When judging one here, use the median and the 5th percentile, or per-channel minima compared like with like; a bare minimum over all channels and lines says nothing about run quality.
  • The “drive coherence goes to exactly 1.0” claim did not reproduce at this scale. Established at 12 drives, it measured median 0.407 with 0.0 % of pairs at exactly 1.0 at 6 drives.
  • Synthetic benchmarks overstated the fast law's speedup — 18–20× on random FRFs against about 3.6× on real data.

Documented defaults that are wrong in the docstrings

  • running_ceiling_db is documented as “default +3.0” in both pseudoinverse_control and buzz_control. The code default is 1e9 — off.
  • The fast law's docstring calls the dB error domain “the default since 2026-09-17”. The executable default is linear.
  • The fast law's docstring lists seven parameter positions; the base class parses ten.
  • Its _restricted_basis table still marks 1e-2 as the default; the shipping default is 2.0 as a multiple, about 3.0e-2 on this frame.
  • match_trace_pseudoinverse's docstring documents three parameters; the parser reads five.
